name: Campus placement (freshers)
summary: Campus placement processes, especially in India, commonly run in stages: an online aptitude test, often with coding or subject questions, a technical interview on your subjects and projects, and an HR round, with a group discussion at some companies. Freshers are usually judged on fundamentals, how clearly they explain their own project, and attitude and communication rather than experience.
rounds: Online test: aptitude (quantitative, logical, verbal), often with coding or subject questions for technical roles
Group discussion for some companies and roles
Technical interview on core subjects, your final-year project and internships
HR round on your background, motivation, relocation and willingness to learn
Some companies combine the technical and HR rounds into one interview
looks_for: Strong basics in your main subjects, not advanced trivia
Owning your project: what you built, why, and what you'd change
Willingness to learn, relocate or work on what the company needs (for many roles)
Honesty: 'I don't know, but here's how I'd work it out'
Teamwork and attitude, shown through college activities

questions.text: Tell me about a team project at college. What was your part, and what went wrong?
covers: The project and the team in a sentence or two
Your own part, separated from the team's
One problem, how it was solved and what you learned

questions.text: Tell me about a time you taught yourself something difficult.
covers: What you learned and why
How you went about it: resources, practice, asking for help
Something you built or achieved with it

questions.text: Describe a responsibility you took on outside your coursework, such as a club, a fest or an internship.
covers: The role and what was expected of you
One challenge and how you handled it
The result, with a number if you have one

questions.text: Tell me about a failure or a poor result at college and what you did next.
covers: What happened, owned honestly
What you think caused it
What you changed and how things went after

questions.text: Walk me through your final-year project: the problem, your part and what you'd do differently.
covers: The problem and why it mattered, in two sentences
Your own part, the tools used and one hard decision
The results, the limits and what you'd change with more time

questions.text: Pick the subject from your degree you're strongest in and explain one idea from it as if to a first-year student.
covers: A clear, simple explanation without jargon
An everyday example
Where it's used in industry

questions.text: Tell me about an internship or training you did. What did you do there yourself?
covers: Where it was and what the team did
Your own tasks and one thing you delivered
What you learned about working in a company

questions.text: Explain the difference between a stack and a queue, and give an everyday example of each.
covers: Stack: last in, first out; queue: first in, first out
Examples such as a pile of plates and a ticket line
Where each is used in software, such as undo or task scheduling

questions.text: What happens, step by step, when you type a website address into a browser? Keep it simple.
covers: Finding the server's address through DNS
Connecting, securely if it's HTTPS, and sending a request
The server's response and the browser showing the page

questions.text: What's the difference between a primary key and a foreign key? Use a college database as your example.
covers: A primary key uniquely identifies each row, such as a student ID
A foreign key links to another table's primary key, such as a student ID in a marks table
Why that link keeps data consistent

questions.text: Which programming language are you most comfortable with, and what have you built in it?
covers: One language, named honestly
Something you built and a problem you solved in it
What you're learning next

questions.text: Estimate how many students in your college bring a laptop to class each day. Talk me through your reasoning.
covers: Starting from total students and splitting by year or branch
Clear, rounded assumptions said out loud
A quick sense-check of the final number

questions.text: Group discussion: 'Should coding be taught in all schools?' Give your opening point and say how you'd bring others in.
covers: A clear stand with one reason and an example
Building on or politely countering what others say
Summarising the discussion if you get the chance
Your education and branch in a line or two
One or two things you've built, led or achieved
Why this company and role fit what you want next

questions.text: Why should we hire you over other freshers?
covers: Two or three strengths, each backed by an example
How they match what the role needs
Willingness to learn, said with a sign you mean it

questions.text: Are you willing to relocate, work in shifts or work on a different technology from the one you studied?
covers: An honest answer, with any real limits stated clearly
Openness to learning, with an example of picking up something new
What you'd want to grow into over time

questions.text: Where do you see yourself in five years?
covers: Growing skills and responsibility in this kind of role
A direction you're interested in, without sounding like you'll leave soon
What you're doing now to get there

questions.text: Do you have any questions for us?
covers: One or two thoughtful questions, such as training, the first project or team
Nothing you could have found on the company's website
A short thank-you

tips: Revise your branch's core subjects (for computer science: data structures, OOP, DBMS, operating systems and networks) and know one programming language well.
Know every line of your CV; interviewers commonly pick a project or skill from it and go deep.
Practise aptitude regularly under time limits; speed comes from practice, not tricks.
In a group discussion, speak early, make one clear point with an example and let others speak; talking over people rarely helps.
Research each company before its pre-placement talk: what it does, its main clients or products, and the role on offer.
If you don't know an answer, say so and explain how you'd work it out; a confident guess usually does more harm.
Outside India, graduate schemes often use online tests, video interviews and assessment centres instead; the same basics and stories still apply.
